summary: The article diagnoses the narrow part of its phenomenon accurately, but its wider point of view is only partly supported, and the analysis could not answer how common the phenomenon is. Whether organisations mostly measure AI transformation by adoption, and how often workarounds occur, rests on assertion, because the article names no study, sample or count and the outside sources do not measure it.

What a usage count records follows from its definition. A count of users, frequency and tokens cannot show how work was completed, so a team running the old process alongside the new one still looks adopted. This holds only for workarounds that keep the tool open. A personal tool used in place of a slow approved tool, or abandonment, would show as low use. The article also uses the word adoption in three senses, which makes its main claim partly true by definition.

The wider claims are weaker. The heading that every workaround shows a design failure goes beyond the article's own team and leadership examples. The claim that people do not adopt AI is the least supported step, though the diagnosis does not need it. The article's first measurement tier, workarounds found and removed, is open to the same shaping by staff that its examples describe, and the article gives no evidence that any tier works.

Trust the narrow usage-count argument and the facts about the text most. The conclusions on the wider claims rest on one article of about 2,050 words with no known date or publisher, and the four outside sources were read only as search summaries. Open questions are how common workarounds are, whether organisations already measure outcomes, and whether the removed-work statement conflicts with the medium-term tier.

conclusions.title: The article names no study, sample or count for its claims about organisations or its workaround examples.
conclusions.text: The only statement about evidence is "These are actual observations from research on tools and agentic automation." It names no study, setting or date. The opening claims that "Boards mostly point AI at cost reduction and customer service, and executives report productivity gains." and that vendors and consultancies follow adoption carry no source or count either.
conclusions.label: none
conclusions.reason: This is a fact about the text, read directly from it. All seven findings report it, and the disconfirmation search found no lines containing the words survey or study. The spot check found 10 of 10 sampled quotations exactly in the article.

conclusions.title: The article uses "adoption" for counted use in one place and for effective use in another.
conclusions.text: Early on it says adoption "counts use: how many people use an app or agent, how often they use its AI features, and how many tokens they consume". Later it says "If adoption means anything at work, it means the tool works well enough, as designed, for people to get the job done with it." The line "adoption is itself a workaround" uses the word in a third sense, as a way of coping while the effect of AI on work is unclear.
conclusions.label: none
conclusions.reason: This is a fact about the text, read directly from it. Definitional analysis listed five usages of the word and fallacy analysis flagged the second as a stipulated definition. Toulmin argument analysis noted the stipulation only as a partly stated warrant.

conclusions.title: The article gives no evidence that its proposed tiers work, and no case where usage matched value.
conclusions.text: It supports the tiers by saying "none of these tiers is new" and that they come from established practice, with no example or result. Its only cases of usage and effective work are cases where the two diverge. It describes no organisation that already measures outcomes and no case where high usage went with good results.
conclusions.label: none
conclusions.reason: This is a fact about the text, read directly from it. The disconfirmation search looked for a counterexample in the article and found none. Historical analogy agrees only in part, because it addresses the closing claim about methods that still work and not the tiers directly.

conclusions.title: The article's tiers name no measure of data quality or of training and support for the work.
conclusions.text: The tiers are tools working as designed, work getting better (time, quality, errors and the experience of staff and customers), people able to do new jobs, and an end state. Data quality appears only as one of the things usage cannot show ("how good its data is"), and training appears as a fix for team workarounds and not as a measure. The article does not claim to give a full account of AI success, so this may be a matter of scope and not an omission.
conclusions.label: none
conclusions.reason: This is a fact about the text, read directly from it. The lens sort found it in both runs, with counts that differ because the items were split differently (information quality had one primary item in the first run and none in the repeat). Absence analysis rated the related absences weak.

conclusions.title: The article's first measurement tier counts workarounds found, which staff who shape their recorded use could distort.
conclusions.text: The short-term tier says "Workarounds found and removed can be reported from the first weeks of a rollout", which is the same early availability the article gives as the reason programs use adoption counts. Its own team and leadership examples describe staff shaping what is recorded, yet the tier does not say how observation and questions would reach workarounds under those conditions. Fewer workarounds could mean a better tool or staff who have learned not to show them. The leadership fix, a statement of how figures will be used, addresses part of this at that level only.
conclusions.label: high
conclusions.reason: Definitional analysis (what counts as a repeatable measure), Toulmin argument analysis (the unstated warrant), fallacy analysis (a double standard) and absence analysis (how workarounds are found without the honesty problem) agree, and they read the text in different ways. Historical analogy and competing hypotheses add only weak support and lean on the METR trial and the vendor survey, which are not relied on for this label. The first run of the lens sort did not raise concealment and its repeat did, which is a difference of scope and not of direction. The repeat of Toulmin argument analysis rated this tier the strongest part of the remedy for being reportable early, while also calling it untested, so it differs in emphasis from the first run, which treated the link from workaround counts to value as the weak point. The internal consistency check found the files consistent on this point and no check failed. The key assumptions check notes that their agreement is one observation seen from several angles.

conclusions.title: The diagnosis is sound in narrow logic but not shown to be common; the point of view is partial.
conclusions.text: What a usage count cannot show follows from what it records, and the article states that part well. How common adoption reporting and workarounds are rests on assertion, and the wider claims (every workaround is a design failure, nobody adopts AI, tiered reporting as the fix) are less well supported than the narrow one. The reasoning is sound for the narrow usage-count argument and has internal tensions elsewhere. The material shows what the article offers for its view and cannot say whether the phenomenon is real.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: All seven techniques point the same way, but this conclusion is built from the conclusions on usage counts, adoption reporting, the design failure heading, removed-work value and the claim that people do not adopt AI, which are each limited to medium. The internal consistency check found that the findings call the reasoning sound while also reporting tensions in it, so the statement is scoped to the narrow argument. The user did not confirm the request after the inference step, so the two-part reading (accuracy of the diagnosis, validity of the point of view) was accepted by the simulated run and not by the user.
conclusions.caveat: It is built from several conclusions that are each only moderately supported, and the findings that call the reasoning sound also report tensions in it, so the statement is limited to the narrow argument. The request was also not confirmed by the user after it was inferred.

conclusions.title: A usage count cannot separate designed use from a workaround that keeps the tool open.
conclusions.text: A count of users, frequency and tokens records that a tool was used and not how the work was completed, so parallel running, repeated attempts followed by finishing by hand, and daily opening to log usage all look like active use. The article's sentence "A workaround does not show up as non-use." is wider than its own examples, because "Or the approved tool is slow, so people use a personal one instead." would appear as low use of the approved tool, and abandonment would too. The claim is also partly true by definition, because the article defines adoption as the opposite of a workaround, which leaves open how often the two diverge.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: Definitional analysis, Toulmin argument analysis, absence analysis and the lens sort agree, and they read the text in different ways (definitions, argument parts, expected items, category counts). Fallacy analysis accepted the factual part but called the definitional step circular, and competing hypotheses rated it consistent with every hypothesis, so it does not discriminate. The label is medium because the internal consistency check found that a call that it is the strongest argument and a call that its definition is circular conflict unless scoped, and the cause is that they judge different parts (the factual count and the definition). This text is scoped that way. The disconfirmation search narrowed the claim to some workarounds and not all, which is applied here. The absence analysis rests on a search summary of the DeLone and McLean model. Both repeat runs agreed on this point.
conclusions.caveat: Two techniques judged the definitional step differently, one calling it circular and one finding it consistent with every hypothesis, and one supporting technique rests on a search summary of a published model. The text is scoped to the factual part to reconcile them.

conclusions.title: That organisations mostly report adoption as AI progress is plausible but not shown.
conclusions.text: The reason the article gives, that adoption "can be counted from the first week of a rollout", is consistent with its claim that value is slow to show in results. It states one direction of influence (vendors and consultancies follow programs), and the text fits the reverse equally well, where seat and usage data arrive with the product. The Microsoft and LinkedIn survey reports that 79% of leaders agree AI adoption is critical to stay competitive, which shows a priority on adoption and says nothing about how progress is measured.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: Definitional analysis, fallacy analysis, absence analysis and the lens sort find no support for prevalence, and they differ in method. Toulmin argument analysis, historical analogy and competing hypotheses find it plausible and do not exclude the rival that organisations already measure outcomes too. The difference is in what each tests (plausibility against support) and is not a conflict of facts. The label is medium because the survey is a vendor source read only as a search summary, so it shows what the vendor reports and not what is true of the world, and the historical comparator is also a search summary. Both are named as limits on this conclusion.
conclusions.caveat: The only outside evidence on this point is a vendor survey, and a vendor survey shows what the vendor reports. Both it and the historical comparison were read as search summaries, and the article itself gives no count.

conclusions.title: The heading that every workaround shows a design failure is wider than the article's own team and leadership examples.
conclusions.text: In the team example nobody has had time to train, so the team agrees to open the tool each day and "then carry on working the old way". In the leadership example a manager makes sure the team records enough usage to stay compliant but not enough to suggest a smaller team. The fixes given for these two are training time and a statement of how figures will be used, which are not changes to the tool. The heading "Each workaround shows where the design failed" holds only if design includes workload and incentives, which the article does not say in this text.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: Definitional analysis, Toulmin argument analysis, fallacy analysis and the lens sort agree, and they read the text in different ways. Historical analogy and absence analysis agree only partly, because they raise other causes (tool performance, lack of training, a workaround that fixes a real fault) without testing these two examples. The label is medium because the internal consistency check found that the findings use the word design in different senses (tool design and a wider sense), so the conclusion depends on which sense is meant. It is stated here for the tool sense. The cause of the conflict is the meaning of design, and the article does not settle it. Both repeat runs agreed that the heading overreaches.
conclusions.caveat: The conclusion depends on what the word design means. The findings used it in two senses and the article does not settle which, so the statement is made for the narrower sense of tool design.

conclusions.title: The article's claim that adoption cannot record removed-work value holds for usage counts, not for measurement in general.
conclusions.text: The article says "An adoption measure has no way to record this value." and this follows for usage counts. It also says "there is no earlier version of the work to compare it with", while its medium-term tier asks programs to track time, quality and errors "compared with how it was done before". A baseline for removed work may exist in earlier request volumes or checking workload, which the article does not mention. Whether the two statements conflict is unresolved, because the findings offer three readings: a defect, a difference of scale (one removed task against a whole piece of work) and sequencing (removed work belongs to the end-state tier).
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: Definitional analysis, Toulmin argument analysis and absence analysis agree, and they differ in method. Fallacy analysis questioned only the claim that this is the "largest" gap, and the lens sort in its first run overstated the comparison problem by applying it to the longer-term tier as well, as the internal consistency check found. The label is medium because of that finding and because the three readings are unresolved. The repeat of Toulmin argument analysis read the two statements as reconcilable, while the first run called it an inconsistency, so the runs disagree on whether it is a defect. They agree that the claim holds for usage counts.
conclusions.caveat: The two repeat runs of Toulmin argument analysis disagreed on whether the article's two statements conflict, and one check found an overstated comparison in another technique. Only the part about usage counts is firm.

conclusions.title: The claim that people do not adopt AI is the weakest step, and the diagnosis does not need it.
conclusions.text: The article offers two cases, a tool with AI built in and a new job, and says "Neither case is adopting AI." It supports this with comparisons to ecommerce, the cloud and web search, and with the statement that AI is "becoming a component of everything", which is a prediction written as present fact. It does not argue that the two cases are complete, and a person who chooses a standalone AI assistant and answers for its output fits neither. The article's own title uses the word it argues against.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: Toulmin argument analysis and fallacy analysis agree, and they differ in method (argument parts against defect patterns). Historical analogy, the lens sort and competing hypotheses agree only in part, because they note that the claim rests on analogy and do not test it. The label is medium because the internal consistency check found that Toulmin argument analysis treated this as a weak point in a chain while fallacy analysis said the point stands without it. The cause is whether the argument is separable. It is treated here as separable from the diagnosis and relevant to the recommendation, which the key assumptions check also concluded. The repeat of Toulmin argument analysis agreed that this is the least supported argument.
conclusions.caveat: Two techniques found the support weak and three others agreed only in part, noting that the claim rests on analogy without testing it. The techniques also differed on whether the argument can be separated from the diagnosis.

conclusions.title: The outside sources fit parts of the article but do not test its workaround claims.
conclusions.text: The METR trial, a randomised study of 16 developers on 246 tasks, found tasks took 19% longer with AI while developers believed it had saved about 20%, so belief and measured result can diverge, in one task type. The Microsoft and LinkedIn survey reports that 78% of AI users bring their own AI tools to work, which fits the article's personal-tool example, and that 39% have had company training. The review of the information technology productivity paradox found evidence inconclusive partly because measures were inadequate, which fits measures being part of the problem and says nothing about workarounds.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: Historical analogy and competing hypotheses use these sources and agree, and the lens sort and absence analysis use only the DeLone and McLean model. The METR trial and the productivity review are research that does not gain from the claim and show what is true of the world, within the limits of 16 developers and one summary. The Microsoft and LinkedIn survey is a vendor source and shows only what the vendor reports. All were read as search summaries, so their wording could not be checked by code, and the label is limited to medium.
conclusions.caveat: Only two techniques used these sources, all four were read as search summaries that code could not check, one is a vendor survey, and the trial covers 16 developers in one task type.

insights.title: The article's proposed replacement has the early availability and exposure to shaping that it faults in adoption counts.
insights.expected: A replacement measure would be expected to answer the weakness it is offered against.
insights.found: Workarounds found and removed can be reported in the first weeks, as adoption can, and the article's own examples show staff shaping what is recorded.
insights.why_it_matters: The first tier could report progress that staff have shaped, and the article does not say how it would avoid this.
insights.label: high
insights.reason: Rests on the conclusion about the first measurement tier, which is high.

insights.title: The article's main claim is partly true by definition, because it defines adoption as the opposite of a workaround.
insights.expected: A reader would expect an empirical diagnosis that evidence could confirm or refute.
insights.found: Under the article's own definition, adoption and workaround exclude each other, so the claim that adoption measures miss workarounds follows from the words. What stays open is how often counted use and effective use diverge, and the article does not show that.
insights.why_it_matters: The diagnosis is hard to refute and says less about practice than it first appears to.
insights.label: medium
insights.reason: Rests on the conclusion about usage counts and workarounds, which is medium, and on the fact about the article's uses of the word adoption.
insights.caveat: It rests on the usage-count conclusion, where the techniques disagreed on whether the definitional step is circular or merely consistent with every hypothesis.

insights.title: Usage counts do show some of the workarounds that the article says they hide.
insights.expected: The request and the article assume usage figures hide workarounds in general.
insights.found: A personal tool used in place of a slow approved tool, and abandonment, would appear as low use of the approved tool. Usage counts hide only workarounds that keep the tool open.
insights.why_it_matters: The blind spot is narrower than the article states, so its size needs evidence.
insights.label: medium
insights.reason: Rests on the conclusion about usage counts and workarounds, which is medium.
insights.caveat: It rests on the usage-count conclusion, which has a definitional step that two techniques judged differently.

insights.title: Two of the article's five workaround levels describe gaming a measure, not routing work around a tool.
insights.expected: All five levels would show the tool failing the person.
insights.found: The team and leadership examples come from workload and incentives, and the article's fixes for them are training time and a statement on how figures will be used.
insights.why_it_matters: Redesigning the tool would not remove the workarounds at those two levels.
insights.label: medium
insights.reason: Rests on the conclusion about the design failure heading, which is medium.
insights.caveat: It depends on the meaning of the word design, which the findings used in two senses and the article does not settle.

not_covered: How common adoption reporting is in organisations, and how often the workarounds the article describes occur. The article names no study, sample or count, and the outside sources do not measure either. This limits the conclusions on prevalence and on the overall diagnosis.
Whether the article's tiers work in practice. The analysis looked for evidence inside the article and in four outside sources and found none, so the tiers are neither supported nor refuted.

Whether the article's statement about removed work conflicts with its medium-term tier. The findings gave three readings (a defect, a difference of scale, sequencing) and the repeat runs disagreed, so this is unresolved.
Whether the heading on design failure is true when design is read to include workload and incentives. The analysis tested it only for tool design, which is the sense the findings could agree on.
Whether staff would in fact hide workarounds under the first measurement tier. This was reasoned from the article's own examples and not tested against any organisation.
The article's date, publisher and audience, which were not supplied, and how the article compares with other writing on measuring AI programs. The analysis worked from the supplied text alone.

The wording of the four outside sources. They were read as search summaries, so code could not check their wording, and the Microsoft and LinkedIn survey is a vendor report that shows only what the vendor says.
The request was not confirmed by the user after it was inferred, and no person reviewed the results.
No recommendation was made, because the request did not ask for one.
basis: Material given by the user: one article, text, about 2,050 words (no link, publisher or date supplied).

Additional source 1: randomised trial of AI tools and developer time (METR), from metr.org, research, used by historical analogy and competing hypotheses, read as a search summary so code could not check its wording.

Additional source 2: Microsoft and LinkedIn survey (78% of AI users bring their own AI tools to work; 39% trained by their company), from microsoft.com, a vendor report, used by historical analogy and competing hypotheses, read as a search summary so code could not check its wording.
Additional source 3: the productivity paradox of information technology review, from ccs.mit.edu, research, used by historical analogy, read as a search summary so code could not check its wording.

Additional source 4: DeLone and McLean information systems success model, from jmis-web.org, research, used by the lens sort and absence analysis, read as a search summary so code could not check its wording.
Analysis techniques that ran, each on the article text: FQ-03, TC1-19, TC1-21, CM1-01, CM1-14, DM-07 and TC1-13. Checks that ran: CH-01, TC1-16 and TC1-18.

Conclusion techniques applied by the synthesis: CF-04 (weighed each line of evidence for reliability and relevance, counting the recurring missing-source point once), UC-01 (stated each uncertainty by what limits it and not by the number of techniques that agree) and UC-06 (linked each label to the techniques, checks and repeat runs behind it). Dropped: UC-02, UC-05, UC-04, CF-08 and CF-09, with reasons in the conclusion picks file.

Report technique applied: RC-02, the limitations and caveats statement, used to link each limitation to the conclusion it weakens in the caveats and in the list of what was not covered. Dropped: RA-01 (no recommendation or audience requested), SA-04 (the fixed summary already answers in plain language), VD-14 (no numbers or charts to show) and RU-08 (no outcome estimates to tabulate).
Combining method chosen in step 7: agreement table and narrative summary, with no pooling.

Checks done: source-span check by code (failures were labels, search terms and text from outside sources, not article quotations); spot check, 10 of 10 sampled quotations exact; repeat runs of DM-07 and TC1-19.
Strength of statement: describe. All chosen techniques can reach describe, and they support all 12 conclusions.
Files that could not be read: none. The article page could not be fetched, so the text was supplied by the user.
Checks not done: no person reviewed the results.

The user did not confirm the request after step 5.1; it was kept as given. For this simulated run the request parts (topic and material scopes, inferred) and permission for outside evidence were accepted in place of the user.
